They compete in [[La Liga]], the [[Spanish football league system|top flight of Spanish football]]. Traditionally, Real Betis play home matches at [[Estadio Benito Villamarín]]. However, since 2025, the club have played their home games at the 70,000-seat [[Estadio La Cartuja]] while awaiting the completion of a €262 million redevelopment of their traditional home.{{Cite web|url=https://www.mirror.co.uk/sport/football/news/laliga-top-10-stadiums-power-13974425|title=We ranked the top 10 stadium in La Liga – with a surprise No.1|last=Jones|first=Rich|date=9 February 2019|website=Mirror|access-date=25 January 2020|archive-date=24 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200124174143/https://www.mirror.co.uk/sport/football/news/laliga-top-10-stadiums-power-13974425|url-status=live}} Real Betis won the league title in [[1934–35 La Liga|1935]] and the [[Copa del Rey]] in [[1976–77 Copa del Rey|1977]], [[2004–05 Copa del Rey|2005]] and [[2021–22 Copa del Rey|2022]]. Given the club's tumultuous history and many relegations, its motto is ''¡Viva el Betis manque pierda!'' ({{lang|es|Long live Betis even when they lose!}}).{{cite news|url=https://www.fifa.com/worldfootball/clubfootball/news/newsid=109997.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090414102617/http://www.fifa.com/worldfootball/clubfootball/news/newsid=109997.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=14 April 2009|title=Real Betis, 100 years of passion|publisher=FIFA|date=18 January 2007|access-date=27 April 2011}} ==History== {{main|History of Real Betis}} The name "Betis" is derived from ''[[Hispania Baetica|Baetis]]'', the Roman name for the [[Guadalquivir]] river which passes through Seville and which the Roman province there was named after. ''Real'' ('Royal') was added in 1914 after the club received patronage from King [[Alfonso XIII]]. ===Foundation=== [[File:Alineación del Real Betis Balompie, 1913..jpg|thumb|right|Real Betis, 25 December 1913]] [[File:Estadio Exposición 1929.jpg|thumb|The grounds of the Estadio de la Exposición (now Benito Villamarín) in 1929]] Betis' city rivals [[Sevilla FC|Sevilla]] were the first club in Seville, founded in October 1905, while a second club, ''España Balompié'' were established in September 1907. "''Balompié''" translates literally as "football", as opposed to the most commonly adopted anglicised version, "''fútbol''". Balompié was founded by students from the local Polytechnic Academy, and were in operation for one year before being officially recognised in 1909 as ''Sevilla Balompié''; despite this, 1907 remains the official foundation date of the club. Following an internal split from Sevilla FC, another club was formed, Betis Football Club. In 1914, they merged with Sevilla Balompié. The club received its royal patronage in the same year, and therefore adopted the name '''Real Betis Balompié'''. Fans continued to refer to the club as ''Balompié'' and were themselves known as ''Los Balompedistas'' until the 1930s, when ''Betis'' and the adjective ''Béticos'' became common terminology when discussing the club and its followers. Real Betis originally played in all blue jerseys and white shorts, for no other reason than the easy availability of such plain colours.{{citation needed|date=April 2019}} However, one of the club's founders and team captain, Manuel Ramos Asensio, was keen to take advantage of his relationships made while studying in Scotland, contacted the Irish-founded Scottish club [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]], whose green and white colours matched the Andalusian regional flag, and obtained the same fabric Celtic used to make kits for his own club. Celtic originally wore green and white stripes but had reoriented a few years earlier to horizontal hoops. Ramos opted for vertical stripes to make the shirts as no other Spanish club used the combination at the time. In 2017 the club officially acknowledged the link with Celtic by producing a special hooped kit to coincide with [[Andalusia Day]].[https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/celtic-tribute-kit-unveiled-real-9831735.amp Celtic tribute kit unveiled by Real Betis for Andalusia Day fixture] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210831143725/https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/celtic-tribute-kit-unveiled-real-9831735.amp |date=31 August 2021 }}, Daily Record, February 16, 2017 The blue colour is still often used in away kit designs.[https://www.footyheadlines.com/2021/07/real-betis-21-22-away-third-kits.html Real Betis 21–22 Away & Third Kits Released] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210831143726/https://www.footyheadlines.com/2021/07/real-betis-21-22-away-third-kits.html |date=31 August 2021 }}, Footy Headlines, July 28, 2021 ===1930s: promotion, championship and relegation=== During the [[Spanish Second Republic]] (1931–1939), royal patronage of all organisations was nullified, and thus the club was known as '''Betis Balompié''' until after the [[Spanish Civil War]] when it would revert to the full name. The club reached the [[Copa del Rey|Copa del Presidente de la República]] final for the first time on 21 June 1931, when it lost 3–1 to [[Athletic Bilbao]] in Madrid.{{cite web|url=https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/spancup1931.html|title=Spain – Cup 1931|website=[[RSSSF]]|access-date=June 8, 2017|archive-date=23 December 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221223114816/https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/spancup1931.html|url-status=live}} Betis marked their 25th anniversary year by winning their first [[Segunda División]] title in [[1931–32 Segunda División|1932]], finishing two points ahead of [[Real Oviedo]],{{cite web|url=https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/spanhist2839.html|title=Spain, Final Tables 1928–1939|website=[[RSSSF]]|access-date=June 8, 2017|archive-date=1 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401050711/https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/spanhist2839.html|url-status=live}} thus becoming the first club from [[Andalusia]] to play in [[La Liga]]. On 28 April 1935, under the guidance of Irish coach [[Patrick O'Connell (footballer)|Patrick O'Connell]], Betis won [[1934–35 La Liga|La Liga]], to date their only top division title. They topped the table by a single point over [[Real Madrid C.F.|Madrid FC]]. A year later Betis went down to [[1935–36 La Liga|seventh]]. This was due to the dismantling of the championship-winning team because of the club's poor economic situation and the arrival of the Civil War, meaning that just 15 months after winning the league title only two players who won in 1935 were left: Peral and Saro. No official league was held during the Civil War between 1936 and 1939, until its resumption for the 1939–40 season and the first year back highlighted Betis' decline as exactly five years after winning the title the club was [[1939–40 La Liga|relegated]]. ===Darkest period=== Despite a brief [[1942–43 La Liga|return to the top division]] which lasted only one season, the club continued to decline and in 1947 an all-time low was reached when the club were relegated to [[Tercera División]]. Many fans see the ten years they spent in the category as key to the "identity" and "soul" of the club. During this time, Betis earned a reputation for filling its stadium and having massive support at away matches, known as the "Green March".{{Citation needed|date=August 2024}} When the side returned to the second level in 1954, it gained the distinction of being the only club in Spain to have won all three major divisions' titles. Much of the credit for guiding Betis through this dark period and back into the ''Segunda'' lies with chairman Manuel Ruiz Rodríguez. ===Benito Villamarín=== In 1955, Manuel Ruiz Rodríguez stepped down from running the club believing he could not offer further economic growth, he was replaced by Betis most famous former president, Benito Villamarín. During his reign Betis returned to the top division in [[1958–59 La Liga|1958–59]] and finished in third place in [[1963–64 La Liga|1964]]. His purchase of the [[Estadio Benito Villamarín|Estadio Heliópolis]] in 1961 is seen as a key point in the history of the club – the grounds were named after him as ''Estadio Benito Villamarín''. In 1965, Villamarín stepped down from his position after ten years at the helm of the club. Just one year after Villamarín's departure, the club would again be relegated to division two, then rising and falling almost consecutively until consolidating their place in the top level in [[1974–75 La Liga|1974–75]]. ===First Copa del Rey Title and European Qualification=== [[File:Manolo Diaz en el Betis 1 (cropped).jpg|thumb|1974–75 Real Betis squad]] On 25 June 1977, Betis played Athletic Bilbao at the [[Vicente Calderón Stadium]] in the [[1976–77 Copa del Rey#Final|Copa del Rey final]]. The match finished 2–2, with Betis winning 8–7 after a staggering 21 [[Penalty shootout (association football)|penalties]] taken to win its first ever Copa del Rey title. This rounded off a solid season in which the club [[1976–77 La Liga|finished fifth in the league]]. After that triumph, Betis [[1977–78 European Cup Winners' Cup|competed]] in the [[UEFA Cup Winners' Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]]: after knocking out [[A.C. Milan|Milan]] 3–2 on aggregate in the first round, the side reached the quarter-finals, where they lost to [[FC Dynamo Moscow|Dynamo Moscow]]. Despite their strong performance in [[UEFA|Europe]], the team [[1977–78 La Liga|suffered league relegation]]. The following year, Betis returned to the top flight and ushered in a period of "good times" for the club, with the next three seasons seeing three top-six finishes, as well as [[UEFA Europa League|UEFA Cup]] qualification in [[1981–82 La Liga|1982]] and [[1983–84 La Liga|1984]]. During the summer of 1982, the Benito Villamarín hosted two matches as part of the [[1982 FIFA World Cup]], and also witnessed the [[Spain national football team|Spain national team]]'s famous [[Spain vs Malta 1984 UEFA European Football Championship qualifying match|12–1 hammering]] of [[Malta national football team|Malta]] to [[UEFA Euro 1984 qualifying|qualify]] for [[UEFA Euro 1984]]. ===Economic crisis and Manuel Ruiz de Lopera=== [[File:Real Betis Balompié league performance 1929-present.svg|thumb|Chart of Real Betis league performance 1929–present]] In 1992, Betis found itself subject to new league rules and regulations due to its restructuring as an autonomous sporting group (SAD), requiring the club to come up with 1,200 million [[Spanish peseta|pesetas]], roughly double that of all the first and second division teams, despite being in level two at the time. In just three months, the fans raised 400 million pesetas with then vice-president [[Manuel Ruiz de Lopera]] stepping in to provide an economic guarantee while himself becoming majority shareholder as the team narrowly avoided relegation. On 11 September 1994, Real Betis played its 1,000th game in La Liga. ===Serra Ferrer success=== {{More citations needed section|date=February 2026}} After another three seasons in the second division, with the club managed by [[Lorenzo Serra Ferrer]], Betis [[1993–94 Segunda División|returned to the top flight]] for the [[1994–95 La Liga|1994–95 season]], subsequently achieving a final third position, thus [[1995–96 UEFA Cup|qualifying to the UEFA Cup]].[[File:Camiseta aniversario betis 001.jpg|thumb|right|Betis' shirts in 2007 bore an emblem for their centenary.]]In the European campaign, Betis knocked out [[Fenerbahçe S.K. (football)|Fenerbahçe]] (4–1 on aggregate) and [[1. FC Kaiserslautern]] (4–1) before losing to [[1996 UEFA Cup Final|defeated finalists]] [[FC Girondins de Bordeaux|Bordeaux]] (3–2). In 1997, 20 years after winning the trophy for the first time, the club returned to the final of the Copa del Rey – again held in Madrid, although this time at the [[Santiago Bernabéu Stadium]] – [[1997 Copa del Rey Final|losing 2–3]] against [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]] after [[Overtime (sports)|extra time]]. Incidentally, ''Barça'' was the club Serra Ferrer would leave Betis for that summer, to be replaced by former player [[Luis Aragonés]]. Aragonés would only last [[1997–98 La Liga|one season]] with the club, leading the side to the eighth position and to [[1997–98 UEFA Cup Winners' Cup|the quarter-finals in the Cup Winners' Cup]], where they would lose 2–5 on aggregate to eventual winners [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]]. Aragonés was followed by the controversial reign of [[Javier Clemente]], who spat on a fan and implied Andalusia was "another country!".{{Citation needed|date=January 2017}} The team slipped down the table, [[1998–99 La Liga|finishing 11th]] and [[1998–99 UEFA Cup|being knocked out of the UEFA Cup]] by [[Bologna F.C. 1909|Bologna]] in the third round. For the next couple of seasons, Betis went through numerous managers, a relegation and a promotion, after which the team [[2001–02 La Liga|finished sixth in the league]] with [[Juande Ramos]] at the helm. Ramos was gone after just one season, however, being replaced by former Cup Winners' Cup-winning manager [[Víctor Fernández]]. He led the team to [[2002–03 La Liga|eighth]] and [[2003–04 La Liga|ninth]] in the league and the [[2002–03 UEFA Cup|third round of the 2002–03 UEFA Cup]], being knocked out by [[AJ Auxerre|Auxerre]] (1–2 on aggregate), during his two-year reign. For 2004, Fernández was replaced by the returning Serra Ferrer, who guided the team to the [[2004–05 La Liga|fourth position in the top flight]]. They also returned to the Vicente Calderón on 11 June 2005 for the [[2004–05 Copa del Rey|Copa del Rey final]], lifting the trophy for only the second time after an extra-time winner by youth graduate [[Dani (footballer, born 1981)|Dani]] in a [[2005 Copa del Rey Final|2–1 win]] against [[CA Osasuna|Osasuna]]. The league finish meant Betis became the first Andalusian team to compete in the [[UEFA Champions League]], and it reached [[2005–06 UEFA Champions League|the group stage]] after disposing of [[AS Monaco FC|Monaco]] in the last qualifying round (3–2 on aggregate). Drawn in Group G, and in spite of a 1–0 home win against Chelsea,{{Cite news |date=2005-11-01 |title=Real Betis 1-0 Chelsea |language=en-GB |work=BBC Sport |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/europe/4387978.stm |access-date=24 April 2022 |archive-date=24 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220424202407/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/europe/4387978.stm |url-status=live }} the club eventually finished third, being "demoted" to the [[2005–06 UEFA Cup|UEFA Cup]], where it would be ousted in the [[2005–06 UEFA Cup knockout stage|round of 16]] by Romanian club [[FC Steaua București|Steaua București]] with a 0–3 home loss.{{Cite web |date=2006-03-16 |title=Steaua thrill in Seville again |url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/news/01b3-0e6d70b9ddd8-da7090e0f81f-1000--steaua-thrill-in-seville-again/ |access-date=2022-04-24 |website=[[UEFA]] |language=en |archive-date=24 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220424202407/https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/news/01b3-0e6d70b9ddd8-da7090e0f81f-1000--steaua-thrill-in-seville-again/ |url-status=live }} Compared to the previous season, the [[2005–06 La Liga|league campaign]] was disappointing, with the club finishing in 14th place, just three points off the relegation zone. ===Centenary celebrations=== [[File:Rgordillo.jpg|thumb|250px|[[Rafael Gordillo]], Betis player and president]] Betis celebrated their [[Century|centenary]] year in 2007. The festivities included a special match against Milan, the [[2007 UEFA Champions League Final|reigning European Champions]], on August 9, with the hosts winning 1–0 thanks to a [[Mark González]] [[Penalty kick (association football)|penalty]] early in the second half. Seven days later, the club won the [[Ramón de Carranza Trophy]] held in neighbouring [[Cádiz]], beating [[Real Zaragoza]] on penalties in the final, having defeated Real Madrid in the semi-finals.{{cite web|url=http://www.realbetisbalompie.es/noticias/comunicados.html?id=3693|title=Todos los partidos de la pretemporada 2007–08|trans-title=All the matches in the 2007–08 preseason|publisher=Real Betis|language=es|date=August 17, 2007|access-date=April 26, 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091230090139/http://realbetisbalompie.es/noticias/comunicados.html?id=3693|archive-date=December 30, 2009}} Surrounding the celebration, it was a time of great change in terms of the playing and technical teams, with eight new signings replacing 14 departures. In the summer of 2006, Serra Ferrer was replaced by [[Luis Fernandez]] for the [[2006–07 La Liga|2006–07]] season. However, the two seasons that encompassed the centenary year (2006–07 and [[2007–08 Real Betis season|2007–08]]) were disappointing, with the club having four different managers and barely avoiding relegation in both seasons.{{Cite web |date=2006-12-21 |title=Irureta says goodbye to Betis |url=https://www.uefa.com/news-media/news/01bc-0f8ea9f3672b-c76c4cca124a-1000--irureta-says-goodbye-to-betis/ |access-date=2022-04-24 |website=[[UEFA]] |language=en |archive-date=24 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220424202359/https://www.uefa.com/insideuefa/national-associations/news/01bc-0f8ea9f3672b-c76c4cca124a-1000--irureta-says-goodbye-to-betis/ |url-status=live }} ===Relegation=== After many years of staving off relegation, Betis' [[2008–09 Real Betis season|2008–09 season]] culminated with a 1–1 draw against [[Real Valladolid]] at home. As a result, the club finished 18th in the table and consequently was relegated to the second division on goal difference.{{Cite web |date=2009-06-01 |title=La Liga's final-day madness ends with riots by Betis fans |url=http://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2009/jun/01/la-liga-real-betis-relegation |access-date=2022-04-24 |website=the Guardian |language=en |archive-date=24 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220424202411/https://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2009/jun/01/la-liga-real-betis-relegation |url-status=live }} On 15 June 2009 over 65,000 ''Beticos'', including icons such as [[Rafael Gordillo]], Del Sol, [[Hipólito Rincón]], [[Julio Cardeñosa]] and others, joined the protest march in Sevilla with the slogan "''15-J Yo Voy Betis''" to let the majority owner Ruiz de Lopera know that it was time to put his 54% share of the club on the market for someone, some entity or the Betis supporters to buy those shares and remove Lopera from the day-to-day operations of the club. Despite the protests, no upper management changes were made during [[2009–10 Segunda División|the season]], which would ultimately see Betis fail to gain promotion back to the top level.{{cite web|url=http://www.elmundo.es/elmundo/2009/06/03/andalucia_sevilla/1244011067.html|title=Lopera sigue mudo y ultras lo amenazan: 'Vende o muere'|trans-title=Lopera still says nothing and is threatened by ''ultras'': 'Sell or die'|publisher=[[El Mundo (Spain)|El Mundo]]|language=es|date=June 3, 2009|access-date=April 26, 2011|archive-date=16 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120116054055/http://www.elmundo.es/elmundo/2009/06/03/andalucia_sevilla/1244011067.html|url-status=live}} ===Lopera court action and sale=== Seville judge Mercedes Alaya was investigating links between Betis and other Ruiz de Lopera-owned businesses, leading to him being formally charged with fraud. On 7 July 2010, one week before the start of preliminary court proceedings, Lopera sold 94% of the shares that he owned (51% of Betis total shares) to Bitton Sport, fronted by Luis Oliver, for the surprisingly low figure of €16 million, leaving Lopera with only minor shares; Oliver had already reportedly taken two football clubs, [[Cartagena FC|Cartagena]] and [[Xerez CD|Xerez]], to the brink of bankruptcy.{{cite web|url=http://www.marca.com/2010/10/27/futbol/equipos/betis/1288188407.html|title=Oliver: "Ni los nazis hacían lo que hace esta loca"|trans-title=Oliver: "Not even nazis did what this crazy woman does"|publisher=[[Marca (newspaper)|Marca]]|language=es|date=October 27, 2010|access-date=April 26, 2011|archive-date=2 February 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110202054459/http://www.marca.com/2010/10/27/futbol/equipos/betis/1288188407.html|url-status=live}} Before the sale could be officially sanctioned, however, Ayala froze Lopera shareholdings. Left with nothing, despite putting down a €1 million deposit, Oliver hastily bought a nominal number of shares from a third party and was voted onto the board of directors by the existing members (all former cohorts of Lopera), allowing him to carry on running the club. In response to this, the judge appointed well-respected former Betis, Real Madrid and Spain national team legend [[Rafael Gordillo]] to administer Lopera's shares to ensure Lopera was not still running the club and that decisions made were for the benefit of the club not individual board members.[http://eldesmarque.es/betis/33746-la-venta-se-cierra-en-16-anos-a-pagar-en-5-anos La venta se cierra en 16 millones a pagar en 5 años (Sold for 16 millions to be paid in 5 years)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309005221/http://eldesmarque.es/betis/33746-la-venta-se-cierra-en-16-anos-a-pagar-en-5-anos |date=9 March 2012 }}; El Desmarque, July 7, 2010 {{in lang|es}} ===La Liga return=== [[File:Deporbetis.jpg|thumb|[[Deportivo de La Coruña]] vs. Betis]] [[File:Captains and referee FC Zenit vs Real Betis, 17 February 2022, UEFA Europa League 02.jpg|thumb|300px|Captain [[Joaquín (footballer, born 1981)|Joaquín]] before an away Europa League fixture in Saint Petersburg in February 2022]] Again under [[Pepe Mel]], Betis started [[2011–12 La Liga|2011–12]] with four wins in as many games, with [[Rubén Castro]] retaining his goal scoring form from [[2010–11 Segunda División|the previous season]], where he scored 27 goals. Betis finished 13th in their first season since returning to La Liga. In the [[2012–13 La Liga|2012–13 season]], Betis finished seventh in La Liga and qualified for the [[2013–14 UEFA Europa League]], the first European qualification for the club since the [[2005–06 UEFA Champions League|2005–06 Champions League]]. This European campaign ended in the quarter-finals after losing on penalties to local rivals Sevilla.{{cite news|title=Spot-on Sevilla get the better of Betis|url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/match/2012664--real-betis-vs-sevilla/|access-date=April 27, 2014|newspaper=[[UEFA]]|date=March 20, 2014|archive-date=23 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140423083308/http://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/season=2014/matches/round=2000471/match=2012664/index.html|url-status=live}} Betis were relegated from La Liga with three games still to play in the [[2013–14 La Liga|2013–14 season]],{{cite news|title=Ronaldo brace sends Real second, Betis relegated|url=https://www.fifa.com/world-match-centre/nationalleagues/nationalleague=spain-liga-2000000037/news/newsid/232/462/5/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140427210756/http://www.fifa.com/world-match-centre/nationalleagues/nationalleague=spain-liga-2000000037/news/newsid/232/462/5/|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 27, 2014|access-date=April 27, 2014|newspaper=[[FIFA]]|date=April 26, 2014}} but [[2014–15 Segunda División|returned immediately as champions]] with two games to spare.{{cite news|title=Real Betis win promotion to Primera Division after Alcorcon victory|url=http://www1.skysports.com/football/news/11827/9864193/real-betis-win-promotion-to-primera-division|access-date=May 26, 2015|work=Sky Sports|date=May 25, 2015|archive-date=26 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150526213747/http://www1.skysports.com/football/news/11827/9864193/real-betis-win-promotion-to-primera-division|url-status=live}} === Back into UEFA competitions === {{More citations needed section|date=February 2026}} In the [[2017–18 Real Betis season|2017–18 season]], under [[Quique Setién]], Betis finished sixth in La Liga and earned a spot in the Europa League. The 2018–19 campaign was very positive; the club reached the [[2018–19 Copa del Rey|Copa del Rey semi-finals]] and topped their group in the Europa League, before eventually being knocked out by [[Stade Rennais F.C.|Stade Rennais]] in the [[2018–19 UEFA Europa League knockout phase|round of 32]]. On 9 July 2020, [[Manuel Pellegrini]] was appointed as Betis manager ahead of the 2020–21 season. He guided them to a sixth-place finish and a Europa League spot, an improvement from 15th the previous season. Betis won the [[2021–22 Copa del Rey|Copa del Rey]] final against [[Valencia CF|Valencia]] after drawing 1–1 after 120 minutes and winning 5–4 on penalties. It was the first trophy for 17 years, since the [[2004–05 Copa del Rey|2005 edition]]. The club displayed consistency under Pellegrini's management by qualifying for the [[UEFA Europa League]] for three consecutive seasons, finishing fifth and sixth in the [[2021–22 La Liga|2021–22]] and [[2022–23 La Liga|2022–23]] seasons, respectively. The club qualified for the [[2024–25 UEFA Conference League|Conference League]] after a seventh-place finish in [[2023–24 La Liga|2023–24 season]] and reached the club's first ever European final the [[2024–25 UEFA Conference League|following season]]. However, they [[2025 UEFA Conference League final|lost]] to [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] 1–4. Betis was able to qualify for the UEFA Champions League for the first time in twenty years following their 5th place finish in the [[2025–26 La Liga|2025–26 season]]. ==Seville derby== [[File:Regatsasevillabetis2009.JPG|thumb|right|Betis and their city rival, [[Sevilla FC]], also compete in an annual rowing race on the [[Guadalquivir]] river.]] {{See also|El derbi Sevillano}} Betis have a long-standing rivalry with city neighbours [[Sevilla FC]]. The two have met 114 times in official competition, with Sevilla holding a 45% win ratio over Betis (31%). The first match between the two clubs took place on 8 February 1915, with Sevilla winning 4–3. The match was not completed, as high tensions led an aggressive crowd to invade the pitch, forcing the [[Referee (association football)|referee]] to abandon the match. In 1916, the first [[Copa Andalucía]] was held, this being the first official derby of the Sevilla area. Of the 17 runnings of the cup, Sevilla were victorious 14 times, to Betis' one sole conquest; this included a 22–0 routing after the latter sent their youth team, in 1918. The first time the teams met in league, in ''Segunda'', happened in 1928–29, with both teams winning their home matches (3–0 and 2–1). They played for the first time in the Spanish top division during the 1934–35 season, with a 0–3 home defeat for Sevilla and a 2–2 draw at Betis, with the latter winning the national championship. On 17 January 1943, Betis lost 5–0 at Sevilla, eventually being relegated. In the first game held at the [[Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium]], on 21 September 1958, the ''Verdiblancos'' won it 4–2. In later years, several matches were also marred by violence, including: a security guard attacked by a Sevilla fan with a crutch (that he did not require to walk), Betis [[Goalkeeper (association football)|goalkeeper]] [[Antonio Prats Cervera|Toni Prats]] being attacked and Sevilla manager Juande Ramos being struck by a bottle of water;{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2007/mar/01/europeanfootball.sport2|title=This was no isolated incident|work=The Guardian|date=March 1, 2007|access-date=April 26, 2011|archive-date=19 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161119100606/https://www.theguardian.com/football/2007/mar/01/europeanfootball.sport2|url-status=live}} the latter incident led to the [[2006–07 Copa del Rey|2007 Copa del Rey match]] being suspended, being played out three weeks later in [[Getafe]] with no spectators. On 7 February 2009 Betis won 2–1 at the Pizjuán, but was eventually relegated from the top flight, while Sevilla finished in third position. Villamarín 2018001.jpg|thumb|right|[[Estadio Benito Villamarín]]]] {{Main|Estadio Benito Villamarín}} Upon Real Betis' formation, the club played at the Campo del Huerto de Mariana. In 1909, Betis moved to the Campo del Prado de Santa Justa, moving to the Campo del Prado de San Sebastián, sharing the site with rivals Sevilla two years later. In 1918, Real Betis moved to the [[Campo del Patronato Obrero]], with the first game at the ground coming against rivals Sevilla on 1 November 1918, resulting in a 5–1 loss for Real Betis. During the 1920s, the ground was redeveloped numerous times by club president [[Ignacio Sánchez Mejías]]. After the construction of the Estadio de la Exposición, the former name of Betis' current home, in 1929, Real Betis moved into the site officially in 1936, after playing a number of games at the stadium since its construction.{{cite web|url=https://espanaestadios.com/2018/08/01/sevilla-campo-del-patronato-obrero/|title=Sevilla – Campo del Patronato Obrero|publisher=Estadios de España|date=August 1, 2018|accessdate=April 27, 2021|archive-date=27 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210427172515/https://espanaestadios.com/2018/08/01/sevilla-campo-del-patronato-obrero/|url-status=live}} With a 60,720-seat capacity, the [[Estadio Benito Villamarín]] is the home ground of Real Betis. It was named ''Estadio Manuel Ruiz de Lopera'' during the 2000s after the club's owner, who decided to build a new stadium over the old one. Despite much planning, the stadium's renovation plans were constantly postponed, and half of it remained unchanged. On 27 October 2010, it returned to its first denomination after a decision by the club's associates.{{cite web|url=http://www.marca.com/2010/10/27/futbol/equipos/betis/1288187951.html|title=De Ruiz de Lopera a Benito Villamarín: el estadio sin nombre|trans-title=From Ruiz de Lopera to Benito Villamarín: the nameless ground|publisher=Marca|language=es|date=October 27, 2010|access-date=April 27, 2011|archive-date=3 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160403174458/http://www.marca.com/2010/10/27/futbol/equipos/betis/1288187951.html|url-status=live}} Due to a major renovation on Estadio Benito Villamarín, Real Betis will play their home matches at [[Estadio de La Cartuja]] from the [[2025–26 La Liga|2025-26 season]] until 2028.{{Cite web|url=https://betismevoycontigo.es/|title=Me voy contigo|website=betismevoycontigo.es|access-date=7 July 2025}} ==Colours== {{Commons|Real Betis Balompié kits}} ===Evolution=== [[File:Betis Copa 3-1.jpg|thumb|right|Betis' green-and-white vertically striped shirts are based on those worn by [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] when an early player was studying in Scotland.]] In its initial years, Sevilla Balompié dressed in blue shirts with white shorts, which represented the infantry at the time. From late 1911, the team had adopted the shirts of [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]],{{cite web|url=http://www.lapalanganamecanica.com/2011/08/los-colores-del-real-betis-balompie.html|title=LOS COLORES DEL REAL BETIS BALOMPIÉ|website=www.lapalanganamecanica.com|access-date=June 8, 2017|archive-date=11 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180211190046/http://www.lapalanganamecanica.com/2011/08/los-colores-del-real-betis-balompie.html|url-status=live}} at that time vertical stripes of green and white, that were brought over from [[Glasgow]] by Manuel Asensio Ramos, who had studied in [[Scotland]] as a child. On 28 February 2017, on the 37th [[Andalusia Day]], Real Betis wore Celtic-inspired horizontal hoops against [[Málaga CF]].{{cite web|url=http://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/celtic-tribute-kit-unveiled-real-9831735|title=Celtic tribute kit unveiled by Real Betis for Andalusia Day fixture|work=Daily Record |date=February 16, 2017|access-date=June 8, 2017|archive-date=17 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170217064004/http://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/celtic-tribute-kit-unveiled-real-9831735|url-status=live}} When the team became Real Betis Balompié in 1914, various kits were used, including: yellow and black stripes; green T-shirts and a reversion to the blue top and white shorts uniform. By the end of the 1920s, Betis was once again sporting green and white stripes, around this time the Assembly of Ronda (1918) saw the Andalusian region formally adopt these colours, not being known how much the two are linked. Since then, this remained Betis' shirt, despite several versions (including wider stripes). Together with the basic green-and-white shirt, Betis has wore both black and green shorts in addition to white shorts.{{Cite web|url=https://www.marca.com/2013/04/18/futbol/equipos/betis/1366277806.html|website=[[marca.com]]|title=La afición elegirá el color del pantalón para el sábado|date=April 18, 2013|access-date=3 August 2021|archive-date=3 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210803001232/https://www.marca.com/2013/04/18/futbol/equipos/betis/1366277806.html|url-status=live}} ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} ==External links== {{Commons category|Real Betis}} * {{Official website|https://en.realbetisbalompie.es/}} * {{Webarchive|title=Real Betis|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150617122933/http://www.laliga.es/en/liga-adelante/betis|url-status=live|website=[[La Liga]]|date=17 June 2015}} * [https://www.uefa.com/nationalassociations/teams/52265--real-betis/ Real Betis] at [[UEFA]] {{Real Betis Balompié}} {{Primera División de España}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Betis}} [[Category:Real Betis| ]] [[Category:La Liga clubs]] [[Category:Men's football clubs in Spain]] [[Category:Football clubs in Seville]] [[Category:Copa del Rey winners]] [[Category:Organisations based in Spain with royal patronage]] [[Category:Association football clubs established in 1907]] [[Category:1907 establishments in Spain]] [[Category:Segunda División clubs]] [[Category:Multi-sport clubs in Spain]]
